title: Io. Argus. Syrinx
source: P. Ovidius Naso, Metamorphoses, ed. Hugo Magnus (Gotha: F.A. Perthes), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0959.phi006.perseus-lat2, sha256 fb3fdb1d8a4a3b82. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Original spelling kept. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: Daphne has just become the laurel, and her father Peneus keeps state in the gorge of Tempe, where the rivers of Thessaly gather at a house that may be in mourning or in honour and cannot tell which. One river is missing: Inachus, weeping for a daughter of his own. Ovid then turns back to tell what happened to her — Jupiter sees Io coming home from her father's stream, drowns the Argive countryside in cloud and takes her by force, and when Juno comes looking he turns the girl into a gleaming heifer. Juno asks for the heifer as a gift and hands her to hundred-eyed Argus to guard, and Io, still herself inside the animal, comes back to her father's bank where she can neither speak nor be known; this part closes with the letter she scratches in the dust with her hoof.

advisory.lede: Jupiter rapes Io in this part, in half a line and in decorous language.
advisory.more: The Latin is 'tenuitque fugam rapuitque pudorem' — he cut off her flight and took her honour by force — and the poem moves straight on to Juno's suspicion. The brevity and the euphemism are Ovid's, not this edition's: the literal translation keeps the Latin's own reticence rather than making the act more explicit than the poem does, or hiding it behind a phrase that would not tell you what happened. Nothing here is softened.

sentences.t:
Est nemus Haemoniae, praerupta quod undique claudit
silva: vocant Tempe.
sentences.l: There is a grove of Haemonia, which a sheer wood closes in on every side: they call it Tempe.
sentences.n: Haemonia is the old poetic name for Thessaly, in northern Greece. 'praerupta ... silva' — adjective and noun stand at opposite ends of the clause with the whole relative clause between them; this splitting (hyperbaton) is normal in Ovid and the reader should get used to hunting the far half of a phrase. 'vocant' with no expressed subject is the impersonal 'they call it' = 'it is called'. Tempe is a Greek neuter plural and indeclinable: the famous gorge of the river Peneus between Olympus and Ossa.

sentences.t:
Per quae Peneus ab imo
effusus Pindo spumosis volvitur undis,
sentences.l: Through which the Peneus, poured forth from the foot of Pindus, is rolled along with foaming waves,
sentences.n: 'Per quae' opens a new sentence with a relative pronoun where English wants a demonstrative: this is the connecting relative, and it means 'and through it'. Ovid uses it constantly to keep sentences chained; whenever a sentence begins quam, quae, quem, qui, try 'and her, and she, and him'. 'quae' is neuter plural because Tempe is. 'ab imo ... Pindo' — the adjective imus names a part of the thing it agrees with, so Latin's 'from lowest Pindus' is English's 'from the foot of Pindus'. 'volvitur' is passive in form and middle in sense, 'rolls itself along'.

sentences.t:
deiectuque gravi tenues agitantia fumos
nubila conducit summisque adspergine silvis
inpluit et sonitu plus quam vicina fatigat.
sentences.l: and by its heavy plunge it draws together clouds that drive thin smokes, and rains with its spray upon the tree-tops, and with its noise wearies more than the neighbouring [places].
sentences.i: The weight of its fall gathers cloud that trails a thin vapour; it rains its spray down on the tops of the woods, and its roar tires out places well beyond its own neighbourhood.
sentences.n: 'tenues fumos' — 'thin smokes': the fine vapour a waterfall throws up, which looks like smoke, and 'nubila agitantia fumos' makes the mist a cloud driving that smoke before it. 'summis silvis' is dative with 'inpluit' ('rains upon'), and summus, like imus in the line above, names a part: 'the tops of the woods'. 'plus quam vicina' compresses a whole clause into three words — 'places more than neighbouring', that is, further off than the immediate neighbourhood. 'inpluit' is the edition's unassimilated spelling of what other texts print as impluit; the edition's orthography is kept as printed throughout.

sentences.t:
Haec domus, haec sedes, haec sunt penetralia magni
amnis;
sentences.l: This is his home, this his seat, these are the inner chambers of the great river;
sentences.n: Three clauses opening with the same word (anaphora), and the verb supplied only at the third: Latin lets 'sunt' do duty for all of them. 'penetralia' is a religious word — the innermost part of a house or temple, where the household gods stand — so the river-god's cave is described as a shrine. 'magni amnis' is held over to the next line, a genitive left hanging across the line-break; Ovid's sentences ignore line-ends and the reader must read on.

sentences.t:
in his residens facto de cautibus antro,
undis iura dabat nymphisque colentibus undas.
sentences.l: sitting in these, in a cave made out of the crags, he was giving laws to the waters and to the nymphs inhabiting the waters.
sentences.i: Seated there, in a cave formed out of the rock, he gave law to his waters and to the nymphs who live in them.
sentences.n: 'iura dare' is the fixed Roman formula for a magistrate dispensing justice — the river-god holds court like a provincial governor, and the joke is that his court is water. 'facto de cautibus antro' — de + ablative for the material something is made out of; the participle 'facto' agrees with antro and English wants a relative clause, 'a cave that had been made'. 'colentibus' from colo, which covers both 'cultivate' and 'inhabit'.

sentences.t:
Conveniunt illuc popularia flumina primum,
nescia, gratentur consolenturne parentem,
sentences.l: There gather first the rivers of his own people, not knowing whether they are to congratulate or to console the father,
sentences.i: The rivers of his own country gather there first, unsure whether to congratulate the father or to console him,
sentences.n: 'Conveniunt' is present where the story is past: the historic present, which Ovid switches in and out of constantly to bring a scene close and then let it go again. Expect present and perfect to alternate with no change of meaning. 'nescia' is neuter plural agreeing with flumina. 'gratentur consolenturne' is an indirect deliberative question — the subjunctive of 'are we to congratulate?' — and the enclitic -ne, tacked onto the second verb, does the work of English 'whether ... or'. 'popularia' is from populus, 'people' (rivers of the same district); do not confuse it with populifer in the next line, which is from the other populus, 'poplar'. They cannot tell which is called for because Peneus' daughter Daphne has just been turned into a laurel: a loss, but also the god Apollo's tree.

sentences.t:
populifer Sperchios et inrequietus Enipeus
Apidanusque senex lenisque Amphrysos et Aeas,
sentences.l: poplar-bearing Spercheus and restless Enipeus, and old Apidanus and gentle Amphrysus and Aeas,
sentences.n: A catalogue of Thessalian rivers, each with one fixed epithet — the technique is Homer's, and the epithets are half the point: the rivers are characters. Amphrysus is the stream where Apollo served as herdsman to king Admetus; Enipeus is the river Neptune impersonated in order to seduce Tyro, which is exactly the kind of thing that is about to happen in this part. 'senex' is a noun used as an adjective, 'old'. 'inrequietus' keeps the edition's unassimilated in- for what is elsewhere printed irrequietus.

sentences.t:
moxque amnes alii, qui, qua tulit impetus illos,
in mare deducunt fessas erroribus undas.
sentences.l: and soon other streams, which, wherever their rush has carried them, lead down into the sea their waters weary with wanderings.
sentences.n: Two relative clauses nested one inside the other: 'qui' (the streams) has 'qua tulit impetus illos' dropped inside it before its own verb arrives. Latin tolerates this stacking; the cure is to find the main verb (deducunt) first and work outwards. 'qua' is the adverbial relative, 'by which way, wherever'. 'fessas erroribus' gives the water a traveller's tiredness, with the ablative giving the cause of the weariness — the first hint of the wandering that will be Io's punishment.

sentences.t:
Inachus unus abest imoque reconditus antro
fletibus auget aquas natamque miserrimus Io
luget ut amissam.
sentences.l: Inachus alone is absent, and hidden away in the depth of his cave he swells his waters with weepings, and, most wretched, he mourns his daughter Io as one lost.
sentences.i: Inachus alone is missing. Sunk deep in his cave, he swells his own waters with his tears, and in utter misery mourns his daughter Io for dead.
sentences.n: Inachus is the river of Argos and Io's father; she will be called 'Inachis', daughter of Inachus, later in this part. A river-god weeping raises the level of his own river — Ovid takes the identity of god and water perfectly literally, and will do so again when Io drinks from muddy rivers. 'imo antro' is once more 'the bottom of the cave' by adjective. 'ut amissam' — ut with a participle gives the ground on which he acts: he mourns her as lost, which also quietly says that he has no proof she is.

sentences.t:
Nescit, vitane fruatur,
an sit apud manes; sed quam non invenit usquam.
esse putat nusquam atque animo peiora veretur.
sentences.l: He does not know whether she enjoys life, or is among the shades; but her whom he does not find anywhere, he thinks to be nowhere, and in his heart he fears worse things.
sentences.i: He does not know whether she is alive or among the dead; but the one he cannot find anywhere he supposes to be nowhere at all, and in his heart he fears worse.
sentences.n: 'vitane fruatur, an sit' is a double indirect question, -ne ... an, 'whether ... or'; and 'fruor' takes the ablative, so 'vita' is not the object but the thing enjoyed. 'quam' is pulled to the front of its clause and then serves as the accusative subject of the infinitive 'esse' — 'her whom he does not find anywhere, he thinks to be nowhere'. The whole point of the line is the pairing usquam / nusquam, 'anywhere' against 'nowhere'. 'manes' are the spirits of the dead, hence the world of the dead.

sentences.t:
Viderat a patrio redeuntem Iuppiter illam
flumine
sentences.l: Jupiter had seen her returning from her father's river,
sentences.n: The pluperfect 'viderat' steps the whole narrative backwards: from here to line 600 Ovid tells what had happened before Inachus began to grieve, and the pluperfects (dixerat, monstraverat, reliquerat) hold the reader in that earlier time. 'a patrio ... flumine' uses an adjective where English wants a genitive ('her father's'), a very common Latin turn — and here it is literal, since her father is the river.

sentences.t:
et “o virgo Iove digna tuoque beatum
nescio quem factura toro,
sentences.l: and 'O maiden worthy of Jove, and destined to make someone-or-other blessed by your marriage-bed,
sentences.i: and 'Maiden worthy of Jove, and sure to make some man or other happy in marriage —
sentences.n: 'nescio quem' is a frozen idiom: the two words have fused into a single indefinite pronoun, 'someone or other', and 'nescio' has stopped governing a question — you can read it as one word. 'Iove digna' — dignus takes the ablative. 'factura' is a future participle, 'about to make, destined to make', and 'toro' (the marriage-bed) is ablative of means. The compliment is already a proposition, and the 'someone or other' whose name he claims not to know is himself.

sentences.t:
pete” dixerat “umbras
altorum nemorum” (et nemorum monstraverat umbras),
sentences.l: seek,' he had said, 'the shade of the high groves' — and he had pointed out the groves' shade —
sentences.i: make for the shade of the tall woods' — and he pointed the shade of the woods out to her —
sentences.n: 'dixerat' is dropped into the middle of the quoted words rather than placed before them: standard practice in Latin verse, and the reader has to be ready for the speech to be interrupted by its own tag. The bracketed clause is the narrator's dry aside — Jupiter does not merely recommend the shade, he indicates it, in case the girl should wander into the wrong wood. Ovid repeats 'nemorum ... umbras' in reversed order so that the gesture mirrors the words.

sentences.t: “dum calet et medio sol est altissimus orbe.
sentences.l: while the heat holds and the sun is at his highest in the middle of his circuit.
sentences.n: 'calet' is impersonal, 'it is hot', with no subject to supply. 'medio ... orbe' is the sun's daily round; at its midpoint he stands highest, so the line means simply 'at noon'. Noon heat is the standing invitation to shade in pastoral and love-poetry, and in Ovid it is regularly the hour at which something happens to a girl who is out alone.

sentences.t:
Quodsi sola times latebras intrare ferarum,
praeside tuta deo nemorum secreta subibis,
sentences.l: But if you are afraid to enter alone the lairs of wild beasts, safe, with a god as your protector, you will go in under the secret places of the groves,
sentences.i: But if you are afraid to go into the beasts' lairs by yourself, you will enter the secret parts of the woods in safety, with a god to guard you —
sentences.n: 'praeside ... deo' is an ablative absolute with no participle at all: two nouns side by side, 'a god (being) protector', which English turns into 'with a god to guard you'. The construction with a participle ('paelice donata' at 622) is everywhere in Ovid, and this participle-less kind is common too; when you meet a bare pair of ablatives that will not attach to anything else, try 'with X as Y'. 'subibis' is sub + eo, 'go up under', the verb for moving into cover. Note what he offers to protect her from: the wild beasts are the smaller danger in this wood.

sentences.t:
nec de plebe deo, sed qui caelestia magna
sceptra manu teneo, sed qui vaga fulmina mitto.
Ne fuge me!”—
sentences.l: and not a god from the common crowd, but [I] who hold the great sceptre of heaven in my hand, but [I] who send out the roving thunderbolts. Do not flee me!'
sentences.i: and no rank-and-file god either, but the one who holds heaven's great sceptre in his hand, the one who looses the wandering lightning. Do not run from me!'
sentences.n: 'qui ... teneo' — the relative pronoun takes a first-person verb because its antecedent is the speaker, so it means 'I, who hold'; English has to insert the pronoun that Latin leaves in the verb ending. 'de plebe' is Roman political vocabulary: the plebs as against the governing order, so Jupiter is claiming senatorial rank among gods. 'vaga fulmina' — the thunderbolt is called 'wandering' because it strikes where it chooses, and the adjective will fit Io before long. 'Ne fuge' is a prohibition with ne + the imperative, an old and poetic alternative to the prose 'noli fugere'.

sentences.t:
fugiebat enim. Iam pascua Lernae
consitaque arboribus Lyrcea reliquerat arva,
sentences.l: for she was fleeing. Already she had left behind the pastures of Lerna and the Lyrcean fields planted with trees,
sentences.i: for she was already running. By now she had left behind the pastures of Lerna and the tree-planted fields of Lyrceum,
sentences.n: 'enim' explains the command we have just heard: the narrator cuts in to tell us why Jupiter said 'do not flee' — she was flying already. The imperfect 'fugiebat' is the tense of action in progress, set against the pluperfect 'reliquerat' for what was finished. Lerna is the marsh south of Argos (later the Hydra's home) and Lyrceum a mountain on the Arcadian border: the flight is mapped across Inachus' own Argive country, so she is running through her father's territory. 'consita arboribus' — ablative of means with the participle of consero, 'sown or planted with'.

sentences.t:
cum deus inducta latas caligine terras
occuluit tenuitque fugam rapuitque pudorem.
sentences.l: when the god, with darkness drawn over them, hid the broad lands, and held her flight, and seized her modesty.
sentences.i: when the god drew a mist down over the wide country and hid it, cut off her flight, and took her by force.
sentences.n: 'inducta caligine' is an ablative absolute, 'with darkness drawn over'. 'cum' with the indicative here is the so-called inverted cum: the sentence looks subordinate but carries the main event, which arrives with no warning. Three perfect verbs, the last two strung on -que ... -que, run the whole act into a single line: he hid, he held, he took. 'rapuit pudorem' is Ovid's decorous phrase for rape — pudor covers both a woman's chastity and the shame of losing it — and nothing softer than rape is meant; the decorum is in the diction only.

sentences.t:
Interea medios Iuno despexit in agros
et noctis faciem nebulas fecisse volucres
sub nitido mirata die,
sentences.l: Meanwhile Juno looked down into the middle of the fields, and, wondering that flying mists had made the face of night beneath a shining day,
sentences.i: Meanwhile Juno looked down over the open country, and, struck that drifting mist had made a face of night under a clear day,
sentences.n: 'medios ... in agros' — medius again does the work of English 'the middle of'. 'nebulas ... fecisse' is an indirect statement depending on 'mirata', with 'nebulas volucres' as its accusative subject: 'that flying mists had made'. 'volucres' is literally 'winged': the clouds move like birds, which is precisely what is wrong with them. The participle 'mirata' does not finish the sentence — it waits for the main verb 'sensit' two lines down. Magnus prints 'agros', 'fields'; some editions print 'Argos', which would have Juno looking down on her own city, since Argos is her town and Io an Argive girl.

sentences.t:
non fluminis illas
esse, nec umenti sensit tellure remitti;
sentences.l: she perceived that they were not of a river, nor were being given off by moist earth;
sentences.n: The indirect statement now hangs from 'sensit', with two infinitives, 'esse' and the passive 'remitti', sharing 'illas' (the mists) as subject. 'fluminis esse' is a genitive of belonging, 'to be a river's'. Juno's reasoning is a naturalist's: mist has two ordinary causes, open water and wet ground, and she can see that neither is there — which leaves an unnatural cause.

sentences.t:
atque suus coniunx ubi sit circumspicit, ut quae
deprensi totiens iam nosset furta mariti.
sentences.l: and she looks around for where her own husband may be, as one who by now knew the thefts of a husband caught out so many times.
sentences.i: and she looks about to see where her husband is — a wife who had long since learned the tricks of a husband caught out so often.
sentences.n: 'ut quae ... nosset' is a causal relative clause with the subjunctive, 'as being one who knew': the construction gives the reason without saying 'because'. 'nosset' is a syncopated novisset, and the perfect of nosco means 'know' (having come to know). 'furta' is literally 'thefts' and is the standing word for a secret love-affair; 'deprensi ... mariti' is a genitive wrapped around the whole phrase, so read to the end before assembling it. 'circumspicit' is present again among past tenses — the historic present speeding up the moment of search.

sentences.t:
Quem postquam caelo non repperit, “aut ego fallor,
aut ego laedor” ait,
sentences.l: And when she did not find him in the sky, 'either I am deceived, or I am wronged,' she says,
sentences.n: 'Quem' opens the sentence as a connecting relative — 'and when she did not find him' (compare 'Per quae' at 569). 'caelo' is a bare ablative of place where prose would write 'in caelo'; verse drops the preposition freely. The line is a sententia, a self-contained epigram: two clauses of identical shape, aut ego ... aut ego, with the two passive verbs fallor and laedor a syllable apart in sound. Juno argues like an advocate setting out two possibilities, and she has already decided which one it is.

sentences.t:
delapsaque ab aethere summo
constitit in terris nebulasque recedere iussit.
sentences.l: and having glided down from the top of heaven she took her stand on the earth and ordered the mists to withdraw.
sentences.n: 'summo aethere' — 'the top of heaven', the same adjective-for-part idiom as imo Pindo (569) and summis silvis (572). 'delapsa' is the perfect participle of a compound of labor, a deponent, so it is active in sense: 'having glided down'. 'iussit' takes an accusative with the infinitive (nebulas recedere), not a ut-clause. Two words carry the goddess from the height of the sky to the ground with no journey described: that is how gods move in Ovid.

sentences.t:
Coniugis adventum praesenserat inque nitentem
Inachidos vultus mutaverat ille iuvencam.
sentences.l: He had sensed his wife's coming in advance, and into a gleaming heifer he had changed the features of Inachus' daughter.
sentences.i: He had felt his wife coming, and had already turned the face of Inachus' daughter into a gleaming heifer.
sentences.n: 'Inachidos' is a Greek genitive of the patronymic Inachis, 'daughter of Inachus'; Ovid keeps Greek case-endings on Greek names throughout the poem, so -os, -on, -a and -an will turn up where a Latin ending was available and refused. 'vultus' is accusative plural — Latin regularly uses the plural for a single face. Both verbs are pluperfect: the change was complete before Juno's feet touched the ground. The metamorphosis itself gets half a line; what Ovid wants is not the change but the life afterwards.

sentences.t:
Bos quoque formosa est. Speciem Saturnia vaccae,
quamquam invita, probat, nec non et cuius et unde
quove sit armento, veri quasi nescia quaerit.
sentences.l: As a cow, too, she is beautiful. Saturn's daughter approves the heifer's looks, though unwilling, and asks besides both whose she is and from where and from what herd she comes, as though ignorant of the truth.
sentences.i: Even as a cow she is lovely. Saturn's daughter approves the heifer's looks — unwillingly — and asks besides whose she is, and where from, and out of what herd, as though she did not know the truth.
sentences.n: 'quoque' here is the plain adverb 'also, too'. Keep an eye on this word: the same letters are often quo-que, the ablative of the relative or interrogative plus -que, meaning 'and by which' — the sense, not the spelling, tells you which you have. 'Saturnia' is Juno, named from her father Saturn; Ovid names gods by descent as often as by name. 'cuius et unde quove sit armento' is a triple indirect question hung on the single verb 'sit'. 'veri nescia' — nescius takes a genitive of the thing not known, and 'quasi' marks the pretence: she knows exactly.

sentences.t:
Iuppiter e terra genitam mentitur, ut auctor
desinat inquiri. Petit hanc Saturnia munus.
sentences.l: Jupiter lies that she was begotten from the earth, so that her origin may cease to be enquired after. Saturn's daughter asks for her as a gift.
sentences.i: Jupiter lies that she was earth-born, to put a stop to questions about her breeding. Saturn's daughter asks for her as a present.
sentences.n: 'mentitur' takes an accusative and infinitive like any verb of saying: 'genitam [esse]', with the esse simply left out, as regularly in verse. 'auctor' of an animal is its origin or breeder, and 'desinat inquiri' puts a passive infinitive under desino, 'may cease to be asked about'. 'munus' is in apposition to 'hanc' — she asks for her 'as a gift', and among Romans a request for a gift is the one form of demand that cannot be refused without insult. That is the trap.

sentences.l: What is he to do? Cruel, to hand over his own love; not to give her, suspicious. There is shame, which would urge from that side; from this side love argues against it. Shame would have been conquered by love;
sentences.i: What is he to do? Cruel, to make his own beloved over to her; suspicious, not to. Shame is what urges him one way, love argues the other. Shame would have gone down before love —
sentences.n: 'Quid faciat' is a deliberative subjunctive: the question a man puts to himself, 'what am I to do?'. 'crudele ... suspectum est' — neuter adjectives predicated of infinitives, which serve as neuter subjects: 'to hand over is a cruel thing'. 'suos amores' is the plural of amor for a single beloved person, standard in Latin love poetry. 'qui suadeat' is a relative of characteristic, subjunctive: the kind of thing that urges. The two sides are worth naming: shame at being exposed pushes him to give the girl up, love pulls the other way — and the sentence gives the verdict ('shame would have been beaten') before the condition that overturns it, which arrives in the next unit.

sentences.t:
sed leve si munus sociae generisque torique
vacca negaretur, poterat non vacca videri.
sentences.l: but if so slight a gift, a cow, were refused to the partner of his stock and of his bed, she could seem not to be a cow.
sentences.i: but if a trifling gift, a cow, were refused to the sharer of his blood and his bed, she might well look like something other than a cow.
sentences.n: An unreal condition: 'si ... negaretur' in the imperfect subjunctive, with 'poterat' left in the plain indicative — Latin often keeps the indicative of possibility in the apodosis, where English says 'she could have'. 'sociae generis torique' says two things at once: Juno is Jupiter's sister and his wife, of his own stock and of his bed. The logic is cold and exact — refusing so small a thing would itself prove the cow was no cow.

sentences.t:
Paelice donata non protinus exuit omnem
diva metum timuitque Iovem et fuit anxia furti,
donec Arestoridae servandam tradidit Argo.
sentences.l: The mistress having been given, the goddess did not at once put off all fear, and she feared Jupiter and was anxious about the theft, until she handed her over to Argus, son of Arestor, to be guarded.
sentences.i: Even with her rival handed over, the goddess did not at once strip off all her fear: she went on fearing Jupiter and worrying about the affair, until she gave her to Argus son of Arestor to keep.
sentences.n: 'Paelice donata' is the ablative absolute in its ordinary participial form — 'the mistress having been given' — where English wants a clause, 'once the rival had been handed over'; compare the participle-less 'praeside deo' at 594. 'paelex' is the harsh word for the other woman, the concubine set against the lawful wife. 'exuit metum' — exuo is to strip off clothing, so fear is something Juno is still wearing. 'anxia furti' takes a genitive of the thing worried about, and 'furtum' is again the stolen love-affair (606). 'servandam' is a gerundive of purpose after tradidit: 'handed over to be guarded'. Arestor is named only to give Argus a father, in the epic manner.

sentences.t:
Centum luminibus cinctum caput Argus habebat:
inde suis vicibus capiebant bina quietem,
cetera servabant atque in statione manebant.
sentences.l: A head ringed with a hundred lights Argus had: from these, in their own turns, two at a time would take rest, the rest kept watch and stayed on post.
sentences.i: Argus had a head encircled with a hundred eyes: of them, taking turns, two at a time would take their rest, while the others kept watch and stayed at their posts.
sentences.n: 'lumina', 'lights', is the poetic word for eyes — the organs by which one sees, named from what they let in. 'bina' is a distributive numeral, 'two apiece, two at a time', not the plain duo; Latin has a separate set of these for things that come in repeated groups. 'suis vicibus' is 'in their own turns', a rota. 'in statione manebant' is military language: a statio is a sentry-post, so the hundred eyes are described as a garrison standing watch in shifts, and the guard is never down.

sentences.t:
Constiterat quocumque modo, spectabat ad Io:
ante oculos Io, quamvis aversus, habebat.
sentences.l: In whatever position he had taken his stand, he was looking towards Io: before his eyes he had Io, however turned away.
sentences.i: However he happened to be standing, he was looking at Io; even facing the other way, he had Io in front of his eyes.
sentences.n: 'Constiterat quocumque modo' is a generalising clause with the pluperfect for indefinite repetition — 'however he had placed himself, on any given occasion'. The name Io is planted twice, once at the end of each clause, exactly as she is planted in front of the watcher. 'aversus' agrees with Argus, not with Io: a creature with eyes all round its head has no back, and 'quamvis aversus' concedes the one thing that would ordinarily help her.

sentences.t:
Luce sinit pasci; cum sol tellure sub alta est,
claudit et indigno circumdat vincula collo.
sentences.l: By daylight he allows her to graze; when the sun is beneath the deep earth, he shuts her in and puts chains around her undeserving neck.
sentences.i: By day he lets her graze; when the sun has gone under the deep earth, he shuts her up and puts a halter round a neck that has done nothing to deserve it.
sentences.n: 'pasci' is passive in form but middle in sense, 'to feed oneself, graze' — the same form governs an ablative in the next unit, 'she feeds on'. 'luce' is a bare ablative of time, 'by day'. 'tellure sub alta' puts the preposition between adjective and noun, normal in verse, and gives the old picture of the sun passing beneath the world at night. 'indigno ... collo' transfers the judgement from Io to her neck: it is the neck that is called undeserving, and the word is the poet's protest, not the guard's.

sentences.t:
frondibus arboreis et amara pascitur herba,
proque toro terrae non semper gramen habenti
incubat infelix limosaque flumina potat.
sentences.l: On the leaves of trees and on bitter grass she feeds, and in place of a couch she lies, luckless, on ground that does not always have grass, and drinks muddy rivers.
sentences.i: She feeds on tree-leaves and bitter grass, and for a bed the luckless creature lies on ground that does not always have so much as grass on it, and drinks from muddy rivers.
sentences.n: 'pascitur' with the ablative — the middle voice again: 'feeds herself on'. 'pro toro' is pro + ablative, 'in place of'; a torus is the couch of a house, and the point is what a king's daughter used to sleep on. 'terrae ... habenti' is dative with 'incubat', 'lies down upon'. 'non semper' is understatement: often not even grass. And the last clause turns the knife — she drinks rivers, and her own father is one.

sentences.t:
Illa etiam supplex Argo cum bracchia vellet
tendere, non habuit, quae bracchia tenderet Argo,
sentences.l: She too, when as a suppliant she wanted to stretch out her arms to Argus, had none that she might stretch out to Argus,
sentences.i: When she wanted to hold her arms out to Argus in supplication, she had no arms to hold out to Argus.
sentences.n: The gesture is the standard one of Roman (and Greek) supplication: the suppliant stretches the arms toward the person begged, and without it there is no way to beg. 'quae bracchia tenderet' is a relative clause of purpose in the subjunctive, 'arms of the sort she might stretch out'. 'cum ... vellet' is cum with the subjunctive describing the circumstance. The sentence says 'bracchia' twice and 'Argo' twice, and the arms are not there either time: the words are all that remain of the gesture.

sentences.t:
et conata queri mugitus edidit ore
pertimuitque sonos propriaque exterrita voce est.
sentences.l: and, having tried to complain, she gave out lowings from her mouth, and took great fright at the sounds, and was terrified by her own voice.
sentences.i: and when she tried to complain, what came from her mouth was a lowing; she took fright at the sound, terrified by a voice of her own.
sentences.n: 'conata' is the participle of the deponent conor and so is active in sense, 'having tried'. 'mugitus' is accusative plural, the bellowing of cattle. This is Ovid's standing pattern for a metamorphosis: the mind survives intact inside a body that will not obey it, and the horror is always the discovery, never the change. 'exterrita ... est' has the two parts of the perfect passive pulled far apart with 'propria voce' between them — read to the end of the sentence before deciding what goes with what. Magnus prints 'et conata queri'; some editions print 'conatoque queri', which attaches the trying to her mouth ('with a mouth that had tried to complain') rather than to Io herself.

sentences.t:
Venit et ad ripas, ubi ludere saepe solebat,
Inachidas ripas;
sentences.l: She came also to the banks where she often used to play, the Inachian banks;
sentences.n: 'et' here is not the connective 'and' but the adverb 'also', standing after the verb: 'she came too'. 'Inachidas' is a Greek accusative plural of the adjective 'Inachian' — Greek endings again on Greek words. The repetition 'ad ripas ... Inachidas ripas' holds the noun up a second time so that the delayed adjective can land: they are not just banks, they are her father's, and her childhood's. Magnus prints 'ripas' in both places; a second witness offers 'rictus', 'gaping jaws', for the second — a very different picture, and the banks are what this edition gives.

sentences.t:
novaque ut conspexit in unda
cornua, pertimuit seque exsternata refugit.
sentences.l: and when she caught sight of new horns in the water, she took fright and, driven out of her senses, fled from herself.
sentences.n: 'nova ... cornua' is split across the line-break with the verb between: the adjective 'new' arrives first and the noun it belongs to is held back to the opening word of the next line. 'ut' with the perfect indicative means 'as soon as'. The point of the sentence is its object: 'seque ... refugit', she flees herself, which is the one flight that cannot succeed. 'exsternata' (the edition's spelling; elsewhere externata) means driven out of one's wits. A reflection in water as the moment of self-recognition is a scene Ovid will build again, most famously for Narcissus in Book III.

sentences.t:
Naides ignorant, ignorat et Inachus ipse,
quae sit; at illa patrem sequitur sequiturque sorores
et patitur tangi seque admirantibus offert.
sentences.l: The Naiads do not know, nor does Inachus himself know, who she is; but she follows her father and follows her sisters, and lets herself be touched and offers herself to those who marvel at her.
sentences.i: The Naiads do not know, and Inachus himself does not know, who she is; but she follows her father and follows her sisters, submits to being handled, and offers herself to their wondering hands.
sentences.n: 'quae sit' is an indirect question governed by both verbs of not-knowing. The Naiads are water-nymphs and daughters of the river, which is why 'sorores' follows without further explanation: they are her sisters, and they pet her as a stranger's animal. 'patitur tangi' — patior with a passive infinitive, 'allows [herself] to be touched'. 'admirantibus' is a participle used as a noun in the dative, 'to those marvelling'. The pathos is exact: everything she does is what a tame heifer would do, and so nobody reads it as anything else.

sentences.t:
Decerptas senior porrexerat Inachus herbas:
illa manus lambit patriisque dat oscula palmis
sentences.l: Plucked grasses old Inachus had held out: she licks his hands and gives kisses to her father's palms
sentences.n: 'Decerptas ... herbas' packs into one participle what English unpacks into a clause, 'grass which he had picked'; Latin does this constantly, and learning to expand a participle into a relative clause is half of reading verse. 'senior' is the comparative of senex used with no comparison intended, simply 'the old man'. 'patriis palmis' is once more the adjective where English wants a genitive, 'her father's'. The tenses do the work: the pluperfect sets the grass in his outstretched hand, and then the presents 'lambit ... dat' bring the scene into the reader's own moment.

sentences.t:
nec retinet lacrimas et, si modo verba sequantur,
oret opem nomenque suum casusque loquatur.
sentences.l: and she does not hold back her tears, and, if only words would follow, she would beg for help and would tell her name and her misfortunes.
sentences.n: A future-less-vivid condition: 'si ... sequantur' with 'oret ... loquatur', all present subjunctive — 'if words should follow, she would beg'. The whole force is in the unreality: they will not follow. 'modo' with the subjunctive gives the wistful 'if only'. 'opem' is accusative of ops, 'help'; the nominative singular of that noun is not used. Note what she would say if she could — help, her name, what happened: the next two lines let her manage exactly one of the three.

sentences.t:
Littera pro verbis, quam pes in pulvere duxit,
corporis indicium mutati triste peregit.
sentences.l: A letter in place of words, which her hoof drew in the dust, carried through the sad disclosure of her altered body.
sentences.i: In place of words, a letter traced by her hoof in the dust carried through to the end the sad proof of her body's change.
sentences.n: 'littera' in the singular is a single written character, not a letter one sends. Ovid does not say which characters she draws, and leaves the reader to see it: the two she can make with a hoof are I and O, which are her name. 'pes' of an animal is the hoof. 'quam' pulls its relative clause inside the sentence, with the antecedent 'littera' standing first for emphasis. 'corporis mutati' is a genitive wrapped around 'indicium', with 'triste' agreeing with indicium — the proof, and it is a sad one. 'peregit' is per + ago, 'carried through to the end', a formal word for completing an official act; writing succeeds where the voice failed.
